report:
# Soursop and Cancer: What the Evidence Shows

**The claim is not supported.** No credible scientific body considers soursop (graviola/Annona muricata) a cure for cancer in humans.

**What the evidence actually shows:**

- **In vitro/lab studies exist, but that's it.** Soursop contains compounds called acetogenins (notably annonacin) that have shown cytotoxic effects against cancer cells in petri dishes and in some animal models. This is where most enthusiasm originates ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/); [Livhospital](https://int.livhospital.com/7-ways-soursop-guanabana-may-help-fight-cancer-benefits-amp-research/)).

- **No human clinical trials demonstrate it cures or treats cancer.** Fact-checkers at PolitiFact, AFP, and Africa Check all reached the same conclusion after consulting oncology experts: lab and animal results have never been replicated in controlled human trials ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/); [AFP Fact Check](https://factcheck.afp.com/scientists-say-there-insufficient-evidence-prove-mangosteen-soursop-and-coconut-water-work-natural); [Africa Check](https://africacheck.org/fact-checks/meta-programme-fact-checks/no-evidence-soursop-leaf-tea-cures-cancer-depression)).

- **Major cancer institutions are explicit on this point.** Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Cancer Research UK both state that despite documented biological activity of soursop's compounds, there is no reliable clinical evidence it treats cancer in people ([Wikipedia summary of MSK/CRUK positions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)).

- **Safety concerns compound the problem.** Annonacin, soursop's key "anticancer" compound, is also a mitochondrial toxin linked to neurotoxicity and an atypical form of Parkinsonism, especially with chronic leaf/seed consumption ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14521988/)).

**Bottom line:** Soursop shows interesting preliminary anticancer activity in lab settings, but the leap to "cures cancer in humans" is not supported by clinical evidence and ignores real toxicity risks. Relying on it in place of proven treatment is discouraged by oncologists.
